mhiTAIL-PCR: A Complete Workflow and Hands-on Experience

Recently, I have been using mhiTAIL-PCR on and off to identify the insertion sites in a batch of Xcc Tn5 mutants. Honestly, it was not nearly as smooth as I had imagined at first. I ran into quite a few problems and spent a good while figuring things out. Later, after I organized the downstream analysis code and uploaded it to GitHub, I thought I might as well turn the wet-lab part into a technical post too—as a complete record for myself and, hopefully, something useful for anyone doing the same kind of work later on.

English translation of the text inside the original image

1. mhiTAIL-PCR identification of genes

  1. Denaturation temperature (refer to the enzyme manual)
  2. Annealing temperature (primer)
  3. Preferably use primers from Invitrogen
  4. Let RuiBo perform the sequencing (sequencing primers can be synthesized by Tsingke)
  5. Colony PCR works less well than genomic DNA

The blue-boxed samples gave good sequencing results. So do not send too many bands for sequencing; once PCR gives a relatively long band, send it for sequencing right away.

This post brings together the primers, reaction mixtures, PCR programs, and a few practical lessons I learned after stepping into various traps. It is suitable for situations where “one end of a sequence is known and the other end is unknown,” such as Tn5 insertion sites, T-DNA insertion sites, transposon-flanking sequences, or genome walking more broadly.

1. How does mhiTAIL-PCR actually find an unknown sequence?

mhiTAIL-PCR was developed by Tan et al. in 2019 as a further improvement on traditional TAIL-PCR and hiTAIL-PCR. Original paper: Tan et al., 2019

The basic idea is actually quite easy to understand:

We already know the sequence at the Tn5 end, so we can design three nested, sequence-specific primers on Tn5 that progressively approach the boundary: RB-0a, RB-1a, and RB-2a.

What we do not know is the genomic sequence outside Tn5. This is where mLAD1–mLAD4 come in. Their 3′ ends contain degenerate bases, allowing them to try annealing to unknown flanking sequences at a lower annealing temperature. Their 5′ ends carry a shared sequence, which is like attaching a “handle” in advance. AC0 and AC1 can then grab this handle and continue the amplification.

The whole process can be roughly divided into three steps:

  1. During pre-amplification, RB-0a extends outward from the known Tn5 sequence, accumulating some single-stranded DNA that contains the unknown flank.
  2. mLAD anneals to the unknown flanking sequence at 25 ℃ and introduces the binding sequence for AC0/AC1.
  3. In the next two PCR rounds, RB-1a and RB-2a—positioned progressively closer to the Tn5 boundary—are used together with AC1 to enrich fragments that truly connect “Tn5 + genomic flanking sequence.”

RB-1a also carries at its 5′ end a tag identical to the shared sequence in mLAD. Shorter fragments are more likely to form a stable hairpin structure, which suppresses their amplification, so longer flanking fragments are more likely to be retained. In the original experiments by Tan et al., the products obtained after adding AC0 were generally longer, and target flanking sequences were recovered in 69 of 72 reactions across the four mLAD primers.

Traditional TAIL-PCR was first proposed by Liu and Whittier. Its core principle also uses nested specific primers, degenerate primers, and alternating high- and low-annealing-temperature cycles to progressively increase the proportion of the target fragment. Liu & Whittier, 1995 Later, hiTAIL-PCR introduced a suppression-PCR design to reduce nonspecific amplification and competition from short fragments. Liu & Chen, 2007

2. The protocol I actually used

1. What do you need before you start?

I used genomic DNA from Xcc Tn5 mutants, diluted to 20–30 ng/μL.

Each sample was paired separately with mLAD1, mLAD2, mLAD3, and mLAD4—four reactions per sample. You can think of it as drawing four cards to improve your odds of hitting a usable flanking sequence.

All primers were diluted to 10 μM working stocks and stored at −20 ℃.

I calculated the Tm values of the specific primers using the NEB Tm Calculator (honestly, this tool is more stable and closer to actual annealing behavior than many other online calculators; it can basically serve as a “reference answer”), and then made small adjustments using a small pilot experiment.

2. Primer sequences

The CGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTG sequence at the 5′ end of RB-1a is an artificially added tag; the latter half is the Tn5-specific sequence.

PrimerSequence (5′→3′)Purpose
mLAD1GCTCACGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTGVNVNNGGAAModified long random degenerate primer
mLAD2GCTCACGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTGBNBNNCCTTModified long random degenerate primer
mLAD3GCTCACGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTGHNHNNAACCModified long random degenerate primer
mLAD4GCTCACGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTGDNDNNTTGGModified long random degenerate primer
AC0GAGCTCACGATGGACTGCUniversal primer for pre-amplification
AC1CGATGGACTGCTGAGTUniversal primer for the next two rounds
RB-0aTCAGAAACAACTCTGGCGCATCFirst Tn5-specific primer
RB-1aCGATGGACTGCTGAGTGGCACCTGAGATTGTCGCACCTGATTGCSecond nested specific primer
RB-2aTCCCGTTGAATATGGCTCATAACAThird nested specific primer

💡 A small practical note
If this tube gives a smear, do not panic. That is normal—you could almost say, “the more it looks like a smear, the more normal it is.”

The 58 ℃ step mainly needs to accommodate the Tm of AC0. If you change AC0, the shared sequence, or the enzyme system, I recommend running a small temperature test again.

After amplification:

👉 Dilute 1 μL PCR product with 50 μL ddH₂O
(This dilution step is critical—do not skip it.)
(Pilot optimization is usually just about fine-tuning this dilution ratio.)

💡 A quick reminder
68 ℃ is the high-stringency annealing temperature for RB-1a, while 50 ℃ allows AC1 to participate in amplification.
The 68 ℃ step essentially determines the specificity. If things go wrong here, the next round usually cannot rescue it.

After amplification:

👉 Dilute 1 μL PCR product with 20 μL ddH₂O
(Pilot optimization is usually just about fine-tuning this dilution ratio.)

ComponentVolume

Diluted primary-round product1.0 μL

(The same three-segment cycling structure is repeated.)

72 ℃   2 min 30 sec
Hold
💡 A quick reminder
65 ℃ is the high-stringency annealing temperature for RB-2a.
If there is still no band in this tube, do not rush to add more cycles. The problem is usually in the first two steps, so it is better to go back and check the recipes and handling of the first two tubes.

6. Gel electrophoresis and sequencing

  • 1% agarose gel
  • Run both the primary- and secondary-round products on a gel
  • Select a clear single band or dominant band for gel extraction
  • Sanger sequencing (bidirectional sequencing with AC1 + RB-2a is recommended)
💡 One very practical note
If you see a band that is “very bright but very short,” do not get excited yet. First suspect that it may be a primer dimer.

The image below shows a batch of samples I actually ran. The upper half used mLAD3, and the lower half used mLAD4; the second- and third-tube products are shown for each sample.

This figure also shows very clearly that the same sample can behave completely differently with a different mLAD primer. Some samples have candidate bands with mLAD3 but not with mLAD4, while the opposite is true for others.

The blue boxes only indicate “candidate bands selected at the time for recovery or sequencing.” Whether a band is the target product must ultimately be determined by sequencing; specificity cannot be judged from the gel image alone.

7. Downstream analysis (you can use the package I wrote!! Highly recommended~)

  • Find the Tn5 end
  • Extract the flanking sequence
  • BLAST against the reference genome
  • Locate the insertion site
  • Perform junction PCR validation when necessary

Below are sequencing results from two representative samples. The junction between the disrupted gene sequence and the EZ-Tn5 transposon sequence can be seen directly in the chromatograms.

If the flanking sequence maps uniquely to the reference genome, the insertion site is usually fairly easy to determine.

If it maps to multiple locations, the flanking sequence may be too short, or the sequence may lie in a repetitive region. You can combine it with the sequencing result from the opposite direction, or redesign a sequencing primer closer to the Tn5 boundary.

I have organized the downstream automated analysis into a package that can identify the Tn5 end, extract the flanking sequence, align it to the reference genome, and organize the insertion-site results.

3. Some practical tips that turned out to be genuinely useful

1. A smear in pre-amplification? Do not panic.

This is one of those things that can really make you question your life choices.

During pre-amplification, mLAD anneals to many different genomic sites at low temperature, so a smear in the first tube is normal. In the original experiments by Tan et al., the pre-amplification products were also smears; clear target bands were progressively enriched during the later nested amplification rounds.

So you do not need to see a beautiful, specific band in the first tube, and there is no need to repeat the experiment immediately just because you see a smear.

2. It is best to run all four mLAD primers

Within the same sample, mLAD1 may give no band while mLAD2 or mLAD4 works very well.

The binding position of mLAD has a random component. Because the four primers have different terminal sequences, running all four can substantially increase the chance of finding a suitable annealing site. In the end, you only need one of them to produce a clear, sequenceable product.

If you have many samples, it is very easy to mix up the mLAD primers while preparing the reactions. I first arrange four groups of tubes for mLAD1–mLAD4, and then add the templates sample by sample.

3. Do not eyeball the two dilution steps

Dilute the pre-amplification product with 1 μL product + 50 μL water; dilute the second-tube product with 1 μL product + 20 μL water.

The dilution is important. It reduces the effects of residual primers, nonspecific products, and high template concentrations from the previous round on the next round. Adding too much product can actually make the third tube develop heavy background or smearing.

If a previously clean system suddenly becomes messy, first check whether the template was accidentally left undiluted or whether the dilution ratios were reversed.

4. Multiple final bands do not necessarily mean failure

mLAD may anneal at different positions, so seeing two or three clear bands in the final product is not unusual.

In this situation, I prefer to gel-extract and sequence the bands separately. Do not judge which band is the target based only on size, because an unknown flank does not have a fixed “correct length.”

If time or budget is limited, start with the clearest band with the lowest background that can be excised cleanly.

5. Be cautious with a very bright short band

If the brightest product is a very short fragment, especially one close to the primer-dimer range, first check whether there is a longer, relatively weaker but still clear band in the same lane.

mhiTAIL-PCR is designed to suppress preferential amplification of short fragments. If you repeatedly obtain only very short bands, check:

  • Whether the 5′ tag on RB-1a is complete;
  • Whether too much AC1 was added;
  • Whether the previous-round product was diluted sufficiently;
  • Whether the high-stringency annealing temperature is too low;
  • Whether the specific primer has obvious nonspecific binding sites.

6. Messy sequencing peaks usually mean the sample is not pure enough

If several PCR products are mixed together and sent directly for Sanger sequencing, overlapping peaks can easily appear from the very beginning.

In that case, rerun the gel and excise the target band more cleanly. Try not to include neighboring bands during gel extraction, and make sure the ethanol is thoroughly removed from the purification column.

If the peaks are still mixed after repeating the gel extraction, consider cloning the product and sequencing individual clones. In the original experiments by Tan et al., gel-purified products could be sequenced directly, but cloning is still a useful backup option for complex samples.

7. If none of the four mLAD primers gives a band

Troubleshoot in the following order:

  1. Check whether other samples from the same batch worked, to determine whether the problem is with one template or the entire batch.
  2. Check whether the genomic DNA is degraded, too concentrated, or contains inhibitors.
  3. Confirm that all three specific primers point outward from Tn5.
  4. Confirm that RB-0a, RB-1a, and RB-2a are progressively positioned closer to the Tn5 boundary.
  5. Recheck the three dilution and template-transfer steps.
  6. Run a small gradient for the high-stringency annealing temperature of the specific primers.
  7. If you want longer fragments, try using a high-fidelity enzyme suitable for long-fragment amplification in the third round as well.

In ordinary PCR, inhibitors in the template, an annealing temperature that is too high, primer-design problems, and insufficient extension time can all cause missing bands; too much template, an annealing temperature that is too low, or too many cycles are more likely to produce smearing and nonspecific bands. The Bio-Rad PCR troubleshooting guide can be used as a reference, but it is best to change only one condition at a time.

8. Deletions or rearrangements may occur near the insertion boundary

If sequencing repeatedly reads only Tn5, or the Tn5 end does not match the expected sequence, the problem may not be PCR alone.

Deletions, duplications, or small-scale rearrangements can sometimes occur near a transposon insertion boundary. Another possibility is that the specific primer is too far from the true junction and the effective Sanger read length begins to decline before reaching the flanking sequence.

In that case, move the final specific primer closer to the Tn5 boundary, or redesign a primer set from the other end of Tn5.

References

  1. Tan J, Gong Q, Yu S, et al. A modified high-efficiency thermal asymmetric interlaced PCR method for amplifying long unknown flanking sequences. Journal of Genetics and Genomics. 2019;46(7):363–366. DOI: 10.1016/j.jgg.2019.05.002
  2. Liu YG, Whittier RF. Thermal asymmetric interlaced PCR: automatable amplification and sequencing of insert end fragments from P1 and YAC clones for chromosome walking. Genomics. 1995;25(3):674–681. PubMed
  3. Liu YG, Chen Y. High-efficiency thermal asymmetric interlaced PCR for amplification of unknown flanking sequences. BioTechniques. 2007;43(5):649–656. PubMed
